just.ai_overall: He describes AI as an engine of economic growth and a national security cornerstone, and he is excited by agricultural AI. His concerns (deepfakes in elections, power demand) read as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a rapidly growing engine of economic growth and a cornerstone of national security, with exponentially rising demand. This suggests large-scale transformation but never mentions AGI.
just.x_risk: His only stated AI risks are everyday ones, such as deepfakes and election integrity, with no catastrophic framing.
just.china_race: He frames AI as a race to lead the world that will be won with reliable, affordable electricity. China is not named, and the race framing appears alongside concerns about energy affordability, so it is present but not dominant.
just.regulation: He applauds the national AI framework and wants to codify it so that states cannot create a patchwork of AI rules. This is a preemption stance against state regulation.

members.summary: Newhouse talks about AI mainly as an economic, agricultural and national-security asset. He focuses on building data centers and the electricity to power them, including Pacific Northwest hydropower. He opposes state-by-state AI rules in favor of a national framework, and his one stated worry is deepfakes and election integrity.

members.name: Glenn Grothman

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly pairs acknowledged benefits (productivity, efficiency, worker safety tools) with concerns about workers, students, privacy and bias. The balance is roughly even, and he asks for careful examination of both sides.
just.agi_pilled: He never addresses how large or lasting AI's impact will be, or AGI. He discusses only specific uses, harms and policies.
just.x_risk: The risks he raises are everyday ones: job displacement, privacy, academic integrity, political bias, deepfakes and electricity costs. None are framed as catastrophic or as loss of control.
just.china_race: China comes up only briefly, as an example of authoritarian AI use (2021), and once in passing as 'As America leads the AI race' in an energy statement. It is not a major lens for his AI policy.
just.regulation: He supports specific rules such as a ban on fake images, data transparency and stewardship rules, and the Ratepayer Protection Act. He also says he wants less regulation than others, that regulation benefits big firms, and that government often fails.

members.summary: Grothman describes AI as having real productivity benefits but also posing risks to workers, students, privacy and political neutrality. He favors careful, targeted steps over broad regulation, such as laws on fake images, data protections and making data centers cover their own energy costs. He is skeptical of heavy regulation and of government competence, and he does not speak about AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Dan Sullivan

just.ai_overall: He says AI has "enormous positive potential" and that its promise in health care and education is "immense and transformative in a very positive way." He pairs this with protecting kids and making AI companies cover their own costs, so he treats risks as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He expects AI to "transform health care, grow our economy" and calls its promise "transformative," which points to broad economic and social change. He never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or human-level AI.
just.x_risk: The risks he raises in his own voice are everyday ones, mainly protecting children online, plus guardrails in general. He does not frame any AI risk as catastrophic or as loss of control.
just.china_race: He repeatedly frames AI as a race against the Chinese Communist Party and ties energy, data centers, and restrictions on investment in Chinese AI to winning it. He still pairs this with guardrails and kids' protection, so the race is not the only lens.
just.regulation: He backs targeted guardrails, especially child protection, and "smart regulation" focused on benefits. He also endorses a uniform national policy that gives innovators certainty, and he supports making AI companies pay their own costs. He does not call for broad licensing, audits, or a new agency.

members.summary: Sullivan talks about AI mainly as an economic and military opportunity, citing health care, education, and Alaska data centers and energy. His most frequent theme is winning the AI race against China, including limiting U.S. investment in Chinese AI. He supports guardrails, especially for children, and a uniform national framework, but does not discuss catastrophic or loss-of-control risks. Several statements in the set (for example s3, s5, s7, s9–s11, s13, s16–s19) read as the Biden-era National Security Advisor Jake Sullivan speaking for the White House, so they were not used.

members.name: Joni Ernst

just.ai_overall: She calls AI helpful in medical research and defense, says we must embrace it, and calls it an exciting area. She also supports guardrails against emerging threats and misuse, so risks are treated as manageable rather than dominant.
just.agi_pilled: She calls superintelligence a powerful tool and treats AI as a major strategic technology, but gives no timelines and does not clearly expect AGI. That fits significant transformation more than an AGI-centered outlook.
just.x_risk: She says Congress must ensure guardrails so superintelligent systems 'cannot go rogue or be misused by our adversaries,' which acknowledges loss-of-control risk alongside misuse. She also flags AI-enabled cyberattacks as a national security threat.
just.china_race: China competition is a recurring, primary lens: she says we cannot pause because China won't, and that America must lead while China races ahead. She still pairs this with calls for guardrails, so it stops short of overriding every other concern.
just.regulation: She supports 'responsible guardrails' that don't stifle innovation, opposes moratoria, and backs targeted measures such as data center cost protections. She expresses no support for broad frameworks or licensing.

members.summary: Ernst speaks about AI mostly in terms of American leadership, national security, and competition with China. She opposes pauses or moratoria and wants to keep innovating. She also backs 'guardrails' against misuse and rogue systems, and wants data centers to pay their own way on power costs.

members.name: Thom Tillis

just.ai_overall: He says directly that "AI is good," calls it a positive disruptive technology, and defends data centers. He also acknowledges real risks and says guardrails are needed, so he is mostly optimistic rather than very optimistic.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is changing quickly and that its future is uncertain, but he never says how large or lasting its impact will be, and never mentions AGI or comparable transformation.
just.x_risk: His own concerns are IP, likeness, cybersecurity, and AI safety incidents. He calls AI an "existential threat to creators," which is a figure of speech about livelihoods, not a catastrophic framing. He rejects the idea that AI concerns are a hoax but does not describe loss of control or catastrophe.
just.china_race: He raises China as an AI-enabled cyber threat and says the US must keep its leadership in AI innovation even if it did not take part. He pairs this with other concerns such as IP, safety, and guardrails.
just.regulation: He mainly backs targeted measures: the NO FAKES Act, IP and copyright protections, disclosure, an AI security incident database, and federal procurement guidelines. He also floats industry self-regulation with codified consequences, but does not call for a broad framework or licensing.

members.summary: Tillis describes AI as a positive, disruptive technology and draws on his long background in it. He supports targeted guardrails, especially for artists' voice and likeness, copyright, and AI security. He pushes back on calling AI concerns a hoax, favors industry self-regulation backed by codified consequences, and supports US innovation leadership and data centers. China appears mainly as a cyber-threat concern.

members.name: Mike Rounds

just.ai_overall: He mostly describes AI as a major opportunity, especially for curing disease, health care, and national competitiveness. He acknowledges threats and dangers but treats them as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He sponsored a bill to create a DoD Artificial General Intelligence Steering Committee, which treats AGI as worth planning for. He also calls AI the 'determining factor in all future great power competition' and says its potential 'hasn't even scratched the surface.' He gives no explicit AGI timelines, so this is a moderate 3.
just.x_risk: He flags national-security risks such as adversaries using AI to develop biological weapons and AI as an attack surface for cyberattacks on critical infrastructure. He does not discuss loss of control or extinction risk.
just.china_race: Beating China is a primary lens for his AI views. He argues against pausing or slowing AI development because China would take the lead, and he says 'we cannot lose this race.' He also mentions kids' safety and guardrails, so it is not fully dominant.
just.regulation: He favors a 'pro-innovative stance,' warns against overly broad rules, and says existing laws already apply to AI. He supports sandboxes, voluntary approaches, and some kids' safety measures, but not broad new frameworks.

members.summary: Rounds speaks about AI mostly as an opportunity, especially for health care and cures, defense, and economic growth, and he frames it as a race the U.S. must win against China. He says it is a mistake to pause AI development and prefers a light-touch, pro-innovation approach with targeted guardrails. He does flag national-security risks such as AI-enabled bioweapons and cyberattacks, and he sponsored a bill creating an AGI steering committee at DoD.

members.name: Trent Kelly

just.ai_overall: He backs AI funding for the military and defends data centers, but he never says how he feels about AI overall, including its benefits and risks.
just.agi_pilled: Neither statement speaks to how big or transformative AI will be, or to AGI.
just.x_risk: He does not discuss any AI risks, catastrophic or ordinary.
just.china_race: He says China wants to lead in AI and data centers and is trying to turn Americans against data centers. This puts China competition in the frame, but it appears in one statement alongside the military-capability point, so it is present but not dominant.
just.regulation: He makes no statement about regulating AI.

members.summary: Kelly talks about AI mainly in terms of national defense and competition with China. He supports funding AI for the military in the NDAA and says China is running a social media campaign against US data centers to get ahead in AI. He says little about AI risks, regulation, or AGI.

members.name: Darin LaHood

just.ai_overall: He calls AI full of promise and a key to the country's future, and he praises beneficial uses such as medical apps. He also acknowledges 'peril' and wants a balance, but opportunity and competition dominate his framing.
just.agi_pilled: He says whoever leads in AI will dominate future warfare, cybersecurity and economic influence, and calls AI 'the future for our country.' That implies a large transformation, but he never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He raises national-security and cybersecurity threats from AI, including adversaries exploiting the technology and data theft. He does not raise loss of control or existential risk. He also worries about harm to children and the elderly, but the national-security framing is the larger-scale concern.
just.china_race: Beating China in AI is his dominant and recurring lens, and nearly all of his statements frame AI that way. He also supports a moratorium because he worries about slowing innovation, and he warns against heavy-handed regulation. His China-focused measures are export and security controls rather than arguments against all rules, so 4 is a close call against 3.
just.regulation: He prefers industry self-regulation and opposes a heavy-handed regime, while allowing a federal role in safety standards, guidelines and protecting vulnerable people. His support for a moratorium (apparently on state laws) and his reluctance to regulate point to a light-touch stance.

members.summary: Darin LaHood talks about AI mostly as a strategic competition with China and a national-security matter. He backs chip-security and anti-adversary AI bills and says the U.S. must win the race. He sees AI's promise, including in health care, and acknowledges some peril. He favors self-regulation and light-touch federal standards, and he supports a moratorium because he worries about slowing innovation.

members.name: Warren Davidson

just.ai_overall: He calls AI one of the most important technologies of our time and says it could boost productivity, but he also warns about surveillance, data exploitation and the need for safeguards. He frames AI as needing both benefits and risks addressed.
just.agi_pilled: He describes AI as 'a freight train in everyone's life' and 'one of the most important technologies of our time,' which points to broad transformation. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He raises a large-scale cyber scenario in which AI breaks bank-level encryption and the banks would have to be shut down. He also urges Congress to act 'while we still can.' He does not discuss loss of control.
just.china_race: He says the US is in a global AI race and wants to win it, but he cautions that the US should not become more like China to do so. The theme appears but is balanced against privacy and civil liberties concerns.
just.regulation: He backs a federal framework that preempts 'harmful' state laws while protecting child safety, fraud and IP, plus privacy legislation and safeguards. He opposed the blanket AI immunity provision in the reconciliation bill and wants AI debated in a standalone bill. He also says it is 'way early' to regulate AI, so his position is targeted rather than comprehensive.

members.summary: Davidson treats AI as a major technology that carries both promise and risk. He puts privacy and civil liberties at the center, calling privacy 'the base layer for ethical AI' and warning about AI-enabled surveillance. He opposed the AI preemption/immunity provision in the big reconciliation bill and wants a standalone, debated bill. He also supports a federal framework and says the US should win the AI race with China without copying China.

members.name: James Comer

just.ai_overall: He frames AI mainly as an opportunity for government efficiency, fraud detection, defense and innovation, and wants to 'unleash AI responsibly'. Risks such as surveillance pricing and privacy are noted but treated as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI 'the next frontier' and a 'transformative technology' that will accelerate and could detect trillions in waste. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His risk concerns are limited to privacy, civil rights, surveillance pricing and regulatory capture. None of these is catastrophic, and he does not address catastrophic risk, so this is closer to ordinary harms. Under the rubric, though, a score of 1 needs him to discuss AI risks and none be catastrophic, which arguably holds here. The statements are thin on risk framing.
just.china_race: He says the US must keep its AI edge and that data centers will be built in China if not in the US. This recurs alongside other concerns such as local control and responsible use.
just.regulation: He supports 'smart regulatory guardrails' but opposes heavy-handed rules and new bureaucracies, and he is wary of the Democratic approach. He does back some targeted transparency and privacy measures for federal AI use.

members.summary: Comer talks about AI mostly as a tool for government efficiency, fraud detection, defense and innovation, and he stresses keeping US leadership over China. He favors light-touch 'smart guardrails' and criticizes new agencies and heavy regulation. He raises specific concerns such as privacy, surveillance pricing and regulatory capture, and does not discuss catastrophic risk or AGI.

members.name: Dwight Evans

just.ai_overall: His only AI-related remarks are negative: he describes AI-driven disinformation as a tactic to disenfranchise Black voters and criticizes a racist AI video. He mentions no benefits, but the evidence is thin and narrow, so this is a tentative low score.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AI's scale, future impact, or AGI.
just.x_risk: He discusses only everyday harms, namely AI disinformation targeting voters and a racist AI video, with no catastrophic framing.
just.china_race: China and AI competition never come up.
just.regulation: He calls for vigilance against disinformation but says nothing about regulation or policy responses for AI.

members.summary: Dwight Evans mentions AI only in the context of harms. He frames AI-enabled disinformation as a tool to suppress Black voters and criticizes a racist AI-generated video posted by President Trump. He does not address AI policy, regulation, competition, or long-term AI futures.

members.name: John Kennedy

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly says AI can make lives better but pairs that with serious warnings about jobs, loss of control, data center costs and hype. The promise and the risk are roughly balanced, and he is also skeptical of the productivity claims.
just.agi_pilled: He describes recursive self-improvement that could turn AI into an independent species that humans can't control, and says even a 1% chance should be taken seriously. He treats this as a real possibility worth planning for, but gives no explicit timelines. He also calls productivity claims hype.
just.x_risk: He says AI could become an uncontrollable independent species that doesn't share human values, and he backs a kill-switch bill. He adds that a 1% chance warrants serious attention. He does not rank it as a top global priority alongside nuclear war, so 3 fits better than 4.
just.china_race: China comes up only in passing: a question about Nvidia chip sales and a jab at Biden over CHIPS Act spending. It is not a recurring lens for his AI policy.
just.regulation: He backs mandatory kill switches on advanced models, AI disclosure requirements, and rules against AI fraud. He says safeguards and accountability don't conflict with innovation. He wants companies, not a government committee, to control the kill switch, and he supports no licensing regime or new agency, so this is substantive but short of the top level.

members.summary: Kennedy is cautiously hopeful about AI, saying it can improve lives, but he is also vocal about dangers ranging from fraud and deepfakes to jobs, data center costs and loss of control. In 2026 he focuses on a kill-switch bill meant to guard against AI that could escape human control, using vivid language such as "Terminator" and "independent species." He favors concrete mandates such as disclosure and kill switches, is skeptical of tech executives and of productivity hype, and rarely frames AI policy as a race with China.

members.name: Margaret Wood Hassan

just.ai_overall: She says AI holds great potential, citing health uses and a push to maximize its potential, but she spends most of her attention on safety, security and scam risks. Promise and risk are roughly balanced.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is advancing rapidly, but she never addresses AGI, superintelligence, or how large or lasting AI's impact will be.
just.x_risk: She raises catastrophic risks such as AI helping terrorists build bioweapons, and says AI could act in unpredictable ways counter to designers' intent. She backs research on making AI safe, interpretable and predictable, which acknowledges a loss-of-control concern. She does not frame this as extinction-level or a top priority.
just.china_race: China comes up repeatedly: export controls, Chinese surveillance AI, and staying the world leader in responsible AI. It is balanced against safety concerns and is not the dominant lens.
just.regulation: She supports balanced oversight of the most advanced AI models, a FedRAMP-style safety evaluation for AI products, and safeguards and standards. She also backs targeted rules on deepfakes. This goes beyond targeted rules but stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Hassan treats AI as a technology with real potential, including in health care and government services, but she focuses mostly on safety and security risks. She stresses scams, deepfakes, bioweapons misuse and unpredictable system behavior, and she pursues bipartisan legislation on AI safety research and oversight of advanced models. She frames China as a security and export-control concern alongside protecting the public.

members.name: Catherine Cortez Masto

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs AI's 'immense potential' and 'incredible innovations' with safety threats and the need for guardrails. Promise and risk get roughly equal weight.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI 'has the potential to profoundly change many aspects of our lives' and that its capabilities 'are growing by the minute.' That implies major transformation, but she never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: She flags AI-enabled threats 'ranging from cybercrime to terrorism' and national-security dangers from AI and advanced chips in adversaries' hands. She does not mention loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: Staying ahead of China recurs across her statements, in the 2018 commission bill, chip export controls, and the call to 'compete with China.' It is balanced with safety and guardrails and does not override them.
just.regulation: She calls for AI safety hearings, global safety and transparency standards, safeguards, and worker protections. She also backs specific measures such as the TAKE IT DOWN Act and anti-bias work. The overall call goes beyond narrow targeted rules, though she does not propose licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Cortez Masto describes AI as a technology with immense potential that also brings growing safety, national-security, and worker-related risks. She calls for guardrails, transparency, global safety standards, and hearings, and also backs targeted measures on deepfakes and housing discrimination. She frames US competition with China and chip export controls as part of AI policy, alongside criticism of the Trump administration for not acting on safety.

members.name: Bradley Scott Schneider

just.ai_overall: He describes AI as both a great opportunity for human advancement and a threat to humanity itself, which is a balanced view with serious risk emphasis.
just.agi_pilled: He worries that frontier models are gaining the ability to break out and act on their own, and calls for safeguards on the most capable systems. This treats highly advanced, autonomous AI as a real near-term possibility, though he never uses the term AGI.
just.x_risk: He calls AI a threat to humanity itself, says frontier models may break out and act on their own, and wants safeguards that keep people in control. That treats loss of control as a real concern. He compares AI to nuclear risk but does not clearly rank it as the top priority.
just.china_race: China appears once, in the line that the U.S. can compete with China while protecting safety. Competition is a minor element and safety is the main framing.
just.regulation: He supports testing and oversight of the most powerful systems, pre-release testing, incident reporting, and meaningful scrutiny of developers. He also wants international guardrails like those for nuclear power. This is substantial frontier-focused regulation, but he does not call for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Schneider describes AI as both a great opportunity and a threat to humanity itself. He focuses on the most powerful frontier systems, citing worries that they could act autonomously and escape human control. He wants testing, oversight, incident reporting and international guardrails modeled on nuclear nonproliferation, and says the U.S. can compete with China while protecting safety.

members.name: Andy Biggs

just.ai_overall: He praises AI as a tool for saving taxpayer money and growing the economy, and he also worries about its use in crime, deepfakes, child exploitation, and national security. Both sides appear without either clearly dominating.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is moving so fast that artificial superintelligence may arrive before 2030, and he asks when algorithms will become the first mover in crime. This treats superintelligence as a near-term possibility, though the remark is partly framed around a question and he doesn't develop it.
just.x_risk: He flags large-scale misuse, including AI combined with drones as a national security threat and AI-enabled criminal exploitation. He does not clearly express concern about loss of control.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an international AI race.
just.regulation: He backs targeted rules, including closing the AI-generated CSAM loophole, age and consent verification for AI sexual content, and remedies for deepfake victims. He also opposes broad federal overregulation, though that is aimed at general regulation rather than AI rules specifically.

members.summary: Biggs presents AI mostly as a useful tool for government efficiency and economic growth, and he opposes broad federal overregulation. He also raises concerns about AI-enabled crime, deepfakes, child sexual abuse material, and national security, and supports targeted fixes for them. In a 2025 hearing he said superintelligence could arrive before 2030, and he has also commented on data center costs and incentives in Arizona.

members.name: Ro Khanna

just.ai_overall: He sees real promise, citing medicine, productivity, and manufacturing, alongside serious harms: job displacement, inequality, and loss-of-control risk. He describes himself as neither an AI doomer nor an accelerationist, which fits a balanced view.
just.agi_pilled: He treats advanced AI that could escape human control as a real concern. He cites a 10% extinction estimate from an Anthropic researcher, warns about recursive self-improvement, and has asked witnesses about AGI timelines. He gives no explicit short timeline, so this stops short of 4.
just.x_risk: He says there is a 'civilizational extinction risk' and a loss-of-control risk, and he compares AI to nuclear war and nuclear power. He calls for a worldwide pause on recursive self-improvement and a federal agency, which makes catastrophic risk a top-tier priority.
just.china_race: China competition recurs in his statements: staying ahead of China, export controls on chips, and leading in AI. He also calls for an AI safety treaty with China and says winning an 'AI war' would be catastrophic. Competition and cooperation are balanced, with cooperation more prominent recently.
just.regulation: He calls for a new federal AI agency modeled on nuclear power and aviation oversight, pre-certification of models, criminal and civil liability, and a pause on recursive self-improvement. He also opposes state-law preemption.

members.summary: Ro Khanna frames AI mainly through workers and economic fairness. He pushes ideas such as taxing automation, a federal jobs program, and a 'worker-first' agenda, while saying AI also has real benefits. In late 2025 and 2026 his rhetoric shifts toward catastrophic and loss-of-control risk, and he calls for a federal AI agency, pre-certification, liability, and an international safety agreement with China. He is hostile to tech billionaires writing the rules and to federal preemption of state AI laws, but he combines this with a pro-innovation, 'stay ahead of China' stance.

members.name: Jimmy Panetta

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly pairs AI's potential (economy, security, local apps) with serious threats and calls for guardrails. This is balanced, with growing emphasis on risk in 2026 statements.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is reshaping the economy, workforce and education, and calls the AI boom significant, but never mentions AGI or superintelligence. This fits a very transformative view without AGI.
just.x_risk: He warns that rapid AI adoption without safety controls could threaten security and safety, and that AI poses risks to 'our country and humanity'. He adopts the concern in his own words, but frames it as security and safety incidents rather than explicit loss of control.
just.china_race: He recurrently cites keeping a competitive edge and staying ahead of rivals like China, while also pushing for safety standards and international coordination. This is a balanced competition theme.
just.regulation: He backs enforceable safeguards, safety standards, transparency, AI testing and reporting, and urges Congress to vote on AI safeguards. This goes beyond narrow rules to a broad federal framework, though not licensing or a pause.

members.summary: Panetta describes AI as an economic and security opportunity, backing investment, workforce programs and local AI innovation. Since 2025 and into 2026 he increasingly stresses serious risks, calling for federal guardrails, testing and enforceable safeguards, and criticizing the Trump administration and House leadership for not acting. He also frames AI in terms of staying competitive with China while seeking global standards.

members.name: Salud O. Carbajal

just.ai_overall: He is enthusiastic about AI research and its potential benefits (new products, a 'technological and industrial revolution'). His only concern is deceptive AI-generated political content, so he leans optimistic with limited risk talk.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is part of a new technological and industrial revolution poised to completely change daily life, which is a transformative framing. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: The only AI risk he raises is deceptive or racist AI-generated campaign content and disinformation, which is an everyday harm. He gives no catastrophic framing.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He condemns deceptive AI-generated content but proposes no rules, laws or regulatory stance on AI.

members.summary: Carbajal speaks about AI mostly in terms of its promise, celebrating federal research funding at UCSB and AI applications such as sustainable materials. He calls AI part of a new industrial revolution. His critical remarks target deceptive, racist AI-generated campaign ads, and he does not discuss regulation, China, or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Nanette Diaz Barragán

just.ai_overall: She sees real benefits (health care, translation, small business tools, access) alongside real harms (bias, errors, disinformation, job loss, data center costs). The two are roughly balanced.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is growing fast and could transform health care. She never addresses AGI or how large or lasting AI's impact will be on society or the economy.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are everyday harms: bias, translation errors, disinformation, job loss, and electricity costs. None are framed as catastrophic or loss-of-control risks.
just.china_race: No statement mentions China or an AI race. The only related line is that America can lead in AI, and it does not address competition with China.
just.regulation: She says Congress needs to regulate AI, opposes a 10-year preemption of state AI laws, and worries about an unchecked industry. She also backs specific measures like worker protections, consumer transparency, and data center cost rules. Taken together this goes beyond targeted rules toward substantial oversight, though she proposes no licensing or new agency.

members.summary: Barragán describes AI as useful, especially in health care, translation, and small business tools, but stresses the need for guardrails. Her concerns are bias, errors, election disinformation, worker protections, and data center costs for families. She says Congress should regulate AI and opposes the preemption of state AI laws, and she does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, or China.

members.name: J. Luis Correa

just.ai_overall: He consistently frames AI as an opportunity, praising student AI projects, encouraging people to explore the technology, and supporting its use in border security. He mentions civil liberties protections only briefly and does not dwell on risks.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AGI, superintelligence, or how large or lasting AI's impact will be. The statements only cover specific uses and student projects.
just.x_risk: He does not discuss catastrophic or existential AI risk. The only harm he mentions is nonconsensual deepfake imagery, which is an ordinary harm, and the rubric requires a broader discussion of risks to score 1.
just.china_race: China appears once, in a remark about Chinese power plants and AI adoption by Chinese businesses. It is a minor, passing point rather than a recurring policy frame.
just.regulation: He supports targeted rules, namely the bipartisan law on removing nonconsensual intimate images, including deepfakes, and he wants civil rights protections alongside AI use in homeland security. He does not call for broad frameworks.

members.summary: Correa speaks about AI in an upbeat, practical way, highlighting local student innovators, encouraging people to explore the technology, and backing AI in border security and homeland security. His one concrete policy statement on harms concerns nonconsensual deepfake imagery, where he supported targeted bipartisan legislation. He mentions China only in passing and does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Lisa Blunt Rochester

just.ai_overall: She repeatedly pairs 'incredible opportunities' with 'unique challenges' and, in 2026, leans toward alarm ('AI is out of control'). Overall her view is balanced between promise and risk.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is disrupting the economy and calls for preparing for the future of work and for AI's growing capabilities, which signals broad transformation without any AGI talk. She does not describe AGI or superintelligence directly.
just.x_risk: She says that even a 1% chance AI could wipe out human life warrants pumping the brakes, and she worries about autonomous hacking and systems that are out of control. This adopts catastrophic and loss-of-control concern in her own voice, though it is not framed as a top-tier global priority.
just.china_race: She says the U.S. cannot afford to lose the global AI race and wants to be the 'winner', but she consistently balances this with environment, safety and national security. Later she criticizes the race as 'out of control'.
just.regulation: She wants states and Congress to be able to regulate, demands accountability and safeguards from frontier AI companies, and calls for hearings and oversight. She also backs targeted bills (fraud, literacy, data center transparency), but her calls for company accountability and safety oversight lean toward substantial rules.

members.summary: Lisa Blunt Rochester describes AI as offering major opportunities in the economy, health and education, and she stresses AI literacy and workforce preparation. Her tone has hardened by 2026, when she calls AI 'out of control', cites a 1% chance of human extinction as a reason to slow down, and presses AI companies on hacking incidents. She also supports winning the AI race and pushes for data center transparency, fraud rules and congressional oversight.

members.name: Neal P. Dunn

just.ai_overall: He calls AI exciting and revolutionary, especially in healthcare, and wants to harness its full potential. He also names misuse risks such as deepfakes, fraud and cyber threats, but treats them as manageable with targeted safeguards.
just.agi_pilled: His own words never address how big or lasting AI's impact will be. The one AGI mention (s13) is a question to a witness, and s15 says only that AI is 'revolutionizing healthcare'.
just.x_risk: He flags national-security and cyber-warfare threats from AI and biodefense concerns. He also voices unease at an experiment in which an AI model blackmailed an engineer. This is mostly misuse and security framing, and he does not clearly endorse loss-of-control risk as a real concern.
just.china_race: Staying ahead of China is a recurring lens for him: competitive edge, chip export controls, CCP threats and 'securing American dominance'. He also supports light-touch regulation, but he does not use the race to argue against all constraints.
just.regulation: He backs targeted measures: deepfake labeling standards, tougher AI fraud penalties and DoD precautions. He also says the US 'must have a light touch on AI regulations' and praises a pro-innovation approach. The overall stance is targeted rules with a light-touch lean.

members.summary: Dunn describes AI as an exciting technology that deserves a light regulatory touch, and he stresses its promise in healthcare and innovation. He supports narrow measures against deepfakes, fraud and cyber risks in defense. He often frames AI through competition with China and national security, and he expressed some concern at an AI blackmail experiment.

members.name: Darren Soto

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly calls AI 'awe-inspiring,' 'incredible,' and critical to economic success, while also flagging disruption, chatbot harms to kids, deepfakes, and rising utility costs. Promise and risk appear in roughly equal measure.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is 'transforming the future of healthcare' and will be an increasing part of daily life, and describes it as an economic driver for the 21st-century economy. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His stated risks are everyday harms: fraud, robocalls, deepfakes, job disruption, chatbot harm to children, and electricity costs. None are framed as catastrophic or loss of control.
just.china_race: He mentions the AI race and global leadership only occasionally ('our rivals will fill that void', U.S. as global leader). China is not a main lens, and the issue is one factor among many.
just.regulation: He backs targeted measures: the AI Accountability Act against deceptive impersonation, limits on kids' chatbot access, AI election safeguards, disclosure and 'rules of the road', and guardrails. He frames this as thoughtful regulation alongside innovation, and does not call for licensing or a broad framework.

members.summary: Soto talks about AI as an economic and innovation opportunity, especially for Central Florida's healthcare, simulation, and chip-manufacturing sectors. He pairs this with concern about everyday harms: chatbots and kids, deepfakes and impersonation, job disruption, and data-center electricity costs. He backs bipartisan, targeted guardrails and consumer-protection uses of AI. He mentions the AI race only occasionally and says nothing about AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Brian J. Mast

just.ai_overall: He calls AI 'the future' and welcomes AI training and investment. His concerns focus on adversaries using AI militarily rather than on AI itself, so he reads as mostly optimistic with manageable risks.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI and other critical technologies will determine economic strength and military power 'for generations to come' and that AI dominance will decide future conflicts. That is transformative framing, but he never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He flags national-security dangers from AI, including military use, AI-powered drones and adversaries getting advanced chips ('real wars, real weapons, real casualties'). He does not discuss loss of control or extinction risk.
just.china_race: The AI race with China is his dominant lens. He chairs hearings on it, writes legislation around it, and publicly attacks Nvidia's CEO over chip sales. He uses the race to argue for tight limits on chip exports, though not against domestic regulation.
just.regulation: He backs specific measures: the AI OVERWATCH Act for congressional oversight of chip sales and export controls on advanced chips. He is also skeptical of Congress's regulatory record, and he states no position on broad AI frameworks.

members.summary: Brian Mast talks about AI almost entirely as a national-security and geopolitical competition with China. He champions export controls on advanced AI chips, including his AI OVERWATCH Act, and criticizes Nvidia's push to sell them to China. He is otherwise upbeat about AI as 'the future,' supporting AI education, training and infrastructure investment, and says little about domestic AI regulation or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Raja Krishnamoorthi

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly pairs AI's promise (scientific breakthroughs, medical help, 'the future of AI is bright') with serious dangers and calls for guardrails. Benefits and risks are weighted roughly equally.
just.agi_pilled: He treats AGI as a real prospect that needs planning. He says AI is 'the defining technology of our lifetimes,' is working on an AGI Safety Act, and notes AI systems improving their own code. He gives no explicit short timelines.
just.x_risk: He says he wants safeguards that keep humans 'firmly in control' of increasingly powerful systems. He also describes rogue-AGI and self-preservation scenarios, wants AGI aligned with human values, and cites Hinton's extinction estimate. He also flags misuse risks to critical infrastructure, biosecurity and nuclear command. He stops short of calling extinction risk his top priority.
just.china_race: Beating China on AI is a recurring and primary lens for him. It drives his chip export controls, the No Adversarial AI Act, and his 'win the AI race' framing. He pairs it with safety and oversight demands and does not use it to argue against regulation, so it falls short of the top level.
just.regulation: He backs substantial rules: independent inspection and validation of frontier models, government oversight during development, enforceable safeguards rather than self-policing, and a bill requiring AGI alignment. He also opposes federal preemption of state AI laws. He does not call for a licensing regime or new agency.

members.summary: Krishnamoorthi describes AI as a powerful, defining technology with real benefits in medicine, science and the workforce, but he stresses its dangers. These include deepfakes and election disinformation, risks to kids, surveillance, and loss of human control over advanced systems and AGI. He frames AI policy heavily around competition with the CCP, through export controls and bans on adversary AI, while also pushing for oversight of frontier models and opposing federal preemption of state AI laws.

members.name: Jim Banks

just.ai_overall: He sees real promise (productivity, economic change 'in really good ways') alongside serious risks (job losses, weaponization, loss of control, national security). The balance reads as roughly even, leaning toward managed optimism.
just.agi_pilled: He compares AI's potential to atomic weapons' paradigm shift and discusses companies pursuing superintelligence that can 'do anything a human can do but much better' as something to plan for. He also says AI will profoundly transform the economy.
just.x_risk: In his own voice he says there are unresolved questions about keeping powerful AI under control. He also wants oversight so models can't build WMDs or autonomously take over systems.
just.china_race: The China race is a dominant, recurring lens. He frames it as a moral, military and economic fight, and he pushes chip export restrictions and workforce measures to stay ahead of China. However, he also supports oversight, so it does not fully override other concerns.
just.regulation: He calls for more federal oversight of frontier models, including internal and undisclosed ones, and backs national security testing against WMD and loss-of-control risks. He also supports chip export restrictions. This goes beyond targeted rules but stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Banks talks about AI mainly through a national security and China-competition lens, calling it a moral and military race the US cannot lose. He acknowledges economic promise and job disruption. In later statements he also voices concern about loss of control, superintelligence and weaponization, and he calls for stronger federal oversight of frontier models.

members.name: Roger Marshall

just.ai_overall: He mostly frames AI as a useful tool and an opportunity in health care, work, and the economy. He also raises concerns about biosecurity, data-center costs, and protecting kids and privacy, but treats these as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is 'transforming our economy and the future of work' and talks about 'the AI era,' which implies broad transformation. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence, and he stresses 'human in the loop' and AI as a tool.
just.x_risk: He calls AI-enabled bioterrorism and the development of novel pathogens or bioweapons his 'biggest concern.' That is a large-scale misuse risk. He says nothing about loss of control.
just.china_race: He says he looks at AI 'first' through a national security lens and that 'we cannot let China get ahead of our military,' calling this 'number one.' China is a primary lens for him, though he still lists other guardrails.
just.regulation: He explicitly favors a 'light touch' and warns against rules that 'destroy innovation.' He does back targeted measures such as transparency, child protection, and privacy, and he supports local data-center moratoriums. Overall he leans light-touch.

members.summary: Marshall describes AI as a practical tool, especially in health care and the workforce, and stresses a 'human in the loop' approach. His main concerns are biosecurity, national security and China, the cost of data centers to ratepayers, and protecting kids and privacy. He favors light-touch, transparency-focused rules and does not discuss AGI or loss of control.

members.name: Clay Higgins

just.ai_overall: He calls AI an "Armageddon level threat" and a tool of government weaponization, though he grants it can be powerful and could serve mankind. Harms clearly dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He never addresses AGI or how large or lasting AI's impact will be. He speaks only of specific uses and threats.
just.x_risk: He calls AI an "Armageddon level threat" worse than a pandemic and says it must be controlled, with humans in charge rather than AI. This suggests loss-of-control concern, though his main framing is government weaponization and authoritarian use.
just.china_race: China and any AI race never come up in his statements.
just.regulation: He supports targeted measures: a bill barring federal use of AI for law enforcement, and a bill protecting constituent communications from automated content. He also says AI should be "effectively controlled." He does not describe a broad framework for regulating AI companies.

members.summary: Higgins mostly describes AI as a threat, especially as a tool for the federal government to surveil or enforce laws against Americans. He has called it an "Armageddon level threat" and introduced legislation to bar federal use of AI for enforcement. He sometimes acknowledges its usefulness, asks about data center energy use, and jokes about AI analyzing rally imagery.

members.name: Mike Johnson

just.ai_overall: He frames AI as a promising technology that needs continued innovation, and says people should not panic. He also acknowledges safety concerns and risks, so he is mostly optimistic with manageable risks.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI could revolutionize industries and is 'posed to transform the world as we know it', which suggests a big transformation. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His risk concerns are everyday or national-security ones (copyright, deepfakes, model safety, 'any technology can be used for evil'), and he tells people not to panic. He does not frame any risk as catastrophic or as loss of control.
just.china_race: He repeatedly invokes China to argue against moratoria, emergency legislation, and hyper-regulation ('we will lose the race to China'). The race framing is used to override regulatory impulses.
just.regulation: He prefers self-regulation, voluntary industry commitments, and a single national framework that avoids state patchworks, and he says to 'regulate only where we must'. He does mention child protection and some oversight, but he is wary of most regulation and opposes a moratorium.

members.summary: Johnson talks about AI as an important, promising technology that America must lead, and he often frames policy around beating China. He opposes moratoria and 'hyper-regulation', prefers industry self-regulation and a single national framework, and says safety and innovation can go together. His concerns center on copyright, deepfakes, model safety, and ratepayer costs, not catastrophic risk.

members.name: Jamie Raskin

just.ai_overall: He calls AI a revolutionary technology that will remake society and wants it to improve public functions, but he stresses surveillance, concentration, and constitutional risks and the need for guardrails. Promise and risk appear in roughly equal measure.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is a revolutionary technology like the telephone, computer and Internet that will remake society, commerce and government, and that it is transforming nearly every industry. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He calls AI a national security and 'human-species security' problem, which is a broad catastrophic-scale framing, and he flags threats to national security and democracy. He does not clearly discuss loss of control, and the 'human-species' quote is undated and brief.
just.china_race: China appears once, in the context of protecting trade secrets and countering IP theft and espionage, and he notes that others call AI an 'arms race.' It is a minor part of his AI discussion.
just.regulation: He backs the Biden executive order's guardrails, opposes the state-law moratorium and preemption, and supports transparency and governance rules. He also supports the task force's recommendations and wants stronger oversight and antitrust action against AI concentration, which is substantial regulation short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Raskin treats AI as a revolutionary, society-reshaping technology and focuses on civil liberties, surveillance, government use, market concentration, and copyright. He strongly opposes a federal moratorium that would preempt state AI laws and favors guardrails, transparency, and the bipartisan task force's recommendations. He often criticizes Musk and the Trump administration over AI, mentions China only in the context of trade-secret theft, and does not discuss AGI or loss of control.

members.name: Jack Bergman

just.ai_overall: His statements address data center siting and costs and ask a question about military AI ethics. None states a general view of whether AI is good or bad.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses how large or lasting AI's impact will be, or AGI.
just.x_risk: No statement discusses catastrophic or existential AI risk. The question about ethics in military AI is too thin to count as a risk framing.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned.
just.regulation: He backs a specific, targeted measure: a one-year moratorium on new AI data centers in Michigan, with local rules and requirements that data centers pay their own way. These are narrow, infrastructure-focused steps rather than a broad framework for regulating AI.

members.summary: Bergman talks about AI mainly through data centers, focusing on local control, utility costs and grid reliability. He supports a temporary Michigan moratorium on new AI data centers and wants data centers to cover their own energy costs. In a 2023 hearing he also asked who is responsible for the ethical and moral implications of AI in the Defense Department.

members.name: Ted Budd

just.ai_overall: He says he is on the optimistic side, believes in AI's promise, and sees humans collaborating with AI. He acknowledges worries but frames them as normal and manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He expects AI to change how jobs are done and treats it as central to economic and national competitiveness. He mentions AGI only in a question about China, so he does not clearly adopt an AGI view himself.
just.x_risk: He flags the prospect of AI-generated biological or chemical weapons in his own voice and sponsored a bill on AI public-health threats. He does not mention loss of control.
just.china_race: Winning the AI race against China is a recurring and primary lens, covering energy, exports, and models. It is paired with calls for light regulation, but he does not say the race overrides every other concern.
just.regulation: He urges caution on new regulation and wants to remove roadblocks and give regulatory certainty to innovators. He also backs a sandbox bill, so he is light-touch rather than strongly anti.

members.summary: Budd speaks about AI as an optimistic opportunity for economic growth and worker empowerment, and he acknowledges public anxieties as normal. His dominant frame is winning the AI race against China, which he ties to energy, permitting reform, and exporting the American tech stack. He prefers light-touch regulation and innovation-friendly policy, and he raises only limited concern about AI-enabled bio/chem threats.

members.name: Don Bacon

just.ai_overall: He mostly frames AI as an opportunity for national security, the economy and health, and tells people to 'lean into AI and oppose the Luddites.' He notes some risks (terrorist exploitation of jailbroken AI, antisemitism amplified by AI) but treats them as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is 'changing the world' and 'reshaping the cyber domain,' and that falling behind in AI would undermine national security. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence, so this is transformative without AGI.
just.x_risk: He raises misuse risks, such as terrorists exploiting jailbroken AI and AI-enhanced cyberattacks, and says guardrails may be needed. He does not discuss loss of control.
just.china_race: The AI race with China is a dominant, recurring lens. He says 'coming in second is coming in last,' calls over-regulation 'a recipe for defeat,' and argues that opposing data centers or regulation helps China.
just.regulation: He is wary of regulation, saying over-regulating AI would cost the US the race, and he opposes 50 different state standards. He does allow for guardrails 'if warranted' and backed an accountability resolution on AI platforms, so he is light-touch rather than strongly anti.

members.summary: Bacon, who chairs the House Armed Services Cyber and AI subcommittee, talks about AI mainly as a national-security and economic competition with China. He is strongly pro-adoption, defends data centers, and warns that over-regulating AI or opposing data centers would hurt the US. He acknowledges misuse risks such as terrorist exploitation and cyber threats, and says guardrails could come later if warranted.

members.name: Josh Gottheimer

just.ai_overall: He repeatedly pairs large expected benefits (health, the economy, science) with serious risks to national security, cybersecurity and kids. Neither side clearly dominates, so his view reads as balanced.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is advancing at 'lightning speed', will transform the economy and is 'changing everything'. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He is concerned about rogue AI agents escaping containment and wants humans kept 'in control' and able to shut agents down. He also flags bioweapon and grid-attack risks from frontier models. He does not frame this as extinction-level or top-tier.
just.china_race: A 'Cold War with China on AI' appears constantly in his statements. He consistently balances it with 'win the right way' and mandatory guardrails, rather than using it to argue against rules.
just.regulation: He backs mandatory government pre-deployment review and testing of frontier models, agent identification requirements, and labeling rules. He rejects voluntary standards and also rejects a pause. He does not call for a new agency or a comprehensive licensing regime.

members.summary: Gottheimer, co-chair of the House AI Commission, describes AI as a major opportunity for health, the economy and science. He stresses its risks even more, especially rogue AI agents, cyberattacks, bioweapons, deepfakes and kids' safety. He frames AI as a Cold War-style race with China that America must win 'the right way', and he backs mandatory pre-deployment government review of frontier models. He rejects both voluntary standards and a pause on AI.

members.name: Jacky Rosen

just.ai_overall: She describes AI's extraordinary potential and uses it in her own work, but also warns of catastrophic damage, scams, surveillance pricing and security threats. The two sides are roughly balanced.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is evolving rapidly and has changed the technology landscape, but she never addresses AGI or how large and lasting AI's impact will be. The evidence is too thin to place her on this dimension.
just.x_risk: She says AI 'can have the power to cause catastrophic damages' without guardrails and calls for executives to testify after the industry said the technology threatens humanity. She frames this as a concern of her own. She also raises misuse risks, but nothing explicit about losing control.
just.china_race: Staying ahead of China is a recurring theme, shown in the DeepSeek bans, the allied AI bill and the call to outcompete China. She pairs it with guardrails and security concerns rather than letting it override them.
just.regulation: She calls for guardrails and safety mechanisms, wants frontier AI executives to testify, and seeks hearings and responsible guardrails on practices like surveillance pricing. She also says 'we're operating in a new world without guardrails.' There is no sign she favors licensing or a new agency, so this stops at substantial but not comprehensive regulation.

members.summary: Rosen, a former computer programmer, talks about AI as a source of real promise (science, wildfire detection, cyber defense) and as a risk. Her concerns include security threats, scams, surveillance pricing, antisemitic output from chatbots, and, more recently, catastrophic harm. She often frames AI through national security and competition with China, including bipartisan bills to ban DeepSeek on government systems. Her later statements push for guardrails and congressional hearings with AI executives.

members.name: Adriano Espaillat

just.ai_overall: He pairs enthusiasm for AI's promise with sustained concern about harms such as election deepfakes, bias and inequity. He says AI "holds incredible promises, but it is also important to address its challenges" and wants to "harness its benefits while putting the right safeguards in place."
just.agi_pilled: He says AI "has the potential to revolutionize our society" and calls AI "NOW," with consequences for future generations. He also frames AI literacy as fundamental as reading and math. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His stated risks are everyday harms: election misinformation, deepfakes, bias, job and workforce effects, and energy costs. He says the election threat is "severe," but this is democratic harm, not catastrophic or loss-of-control risk.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race in an AI context.
just.regulation: He backs targeted rules: his bill on AI in political ads, transparency requirements, bias and accountability measures, and oversight of AI in housing and finance. He says "We must govern and regulate AI before it's too late" and notes that Congress has yet to act on automated systems. He does not call for a broad licensing framework or a new agency.

members.summary: Espaillat talks about AI mainly through election integrity, equity and inclusion for Latino and minority communities, and AI literacy. He sponsored a bill on AI-generated political ads and hosted Hispanic Caucus roundtables. He describes AI as a promising, revolutionary technology that needs safeguards, bipartisan work and responsible development. He does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk or China.

members.name: Brian K. Fitzpatrick

just.ai_overall: He calls AI an 'enormous opportunity and equally serious questions' and wants to 'embrace innovation without abandoning responsibility.' He balances promotion of AI investment with concern about security, workers and deepfakes.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI 'reshapes the future of work' and calls a data center project 'transformational.' He also says AI capabilities are accelerating. He never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He flags national-security risks from accelerating AI, including threats to critical infrastructure, AI-enabled cyber aggression, and an AI-run espionage operation. He does not mention loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: Staying ahead of China and adversaries recurs in his national security and standards-setting statements. It is balanced by calls for international safety frameworks, worker protections and oversight, so it is not the dominant lens.
just.regulation: He pushes dozens of bipartisan bills on AI security, transparency and independent oversight. He also backs safety testing and incident-reporting standards and accountability, which goes beyond narrow targeted rules. He is not calling for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Fitzpatrick presents AI as both a major opportunity and a serious security and workforce challenge. He supports local AI data center investment and U.S. leadership. He also champions bipartisan bills on deepfakes, election integrity, AI security, transparency and oversight, and worker-centered AI policy. His risk language focuses on national security, cyber threats and China, not on loss of control.

members.name: Lloyd Smucker

just.ai_overall: He says America should lead the world in AI and frames the main concern as data center energy costs falling on ratepayers, which he treats as manageable. His other remarks are about letting the market develop AI, which points to an optimistic lean without enthusiasm.
just.agi_pilled: None of the statements address how large or transformative AI will be, or mention AGI.
just.x_risk: He does not discuss catastrophic or existential AI risks, or any other AI harms, in his own voice.
just.china_race: He says America should lead the world in AI, but China and an AI race are never mentioned, so the statements do not show a China-race framing.
just.regulation: He calls government rule-setting for AI the worst possible thing, wants the market to decide, and objects to a 50-state patchwork. This matches the strongly anti-regulation and preemption-leaning level, though he backs a narrow ratepayer bill on data center costs.

members.summary: Smucker favors American leadership in AI and prefers market-led development to government rule-setting. He objects to a patchwork of state regulations and says government bureaucrats should not set the rules for AI. He does back a narrow ratepayer bill so data centers pay their own energy costs. He says nothing about AGI, catastrophic risk, or China.

members.name: David Kustoff

just.ai_overall: He celebrates AI investment and student AI projects as opportunities for Memphis and the economy, and treats AI-enabled robocall fraud as a specific harm to be policed. The tone is mainly optimistic with only narrow risks mentioned.
just.agi_pilled: He says the xAI investment will lead 'into the next generation of technology' and make Memphis a 'global hub for artificial intelligence.' That implies a large economic shift, but he never mentions AGI or human-level AI.
just.x_risk: The only risks he discusses are everyday harms such as AI-voiced robocall scams and fraud. He gives no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: He mentions only 'U.S. dominance' in AI when listing the Trump AI Action Plan among administration wins. China does not feature as an AI competitor in his own words.
just.regulation: He backs narrow, targeted measures against AI-enabled robocall fraud, such as the DO NOT Call Act and higher penalties. He does not endorse broad AI regulation.

members.summary: Kustoff talks about AI mostly as an economic opportunity, especially the xAI supercomputer investment in Memphis, and he praises student AI projects. His main concern is AI-enabled robocall scams, which he addresses with targeted legislation. He does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, or broad AI regulation, and he mentions AI dominance only in passing.

members.name: Vicente Gonzalez

just.ai_overall: He sees AI as an economic opportunity (new industry for Corpus Christi, and he cites a projected GDP boost), but also worries about AI-enabled scams targeting seniors. The evidence is thin, so a mixed score fits best.
just.agi_pilled: He never addresses how big or transformative AI will be. He cites a GDP projection (s1), but that is a report's estimate and he does not clearly adopt it as his own view of AI's scale.
just.x_risk: The only risks he raises are everyday harms, namely scams that target seniors (including impersonation calls). None are catastrophic.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He calls for public awareness of scams but says nothing about AI regulation or legislation.

members.summary: Gonzalez talks about AI mostly in local economic and consumer-protection terms. He sees it as a source of new industry and economic growth, and he is concerned about AI-enabled scams that target seniors. He also mocks the President's use of AI-generated imagery. He does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, China, or regulation in these statements.

members.name: Jodey C. Arrington

just.ai_overall: He frames AI mainly as an economic and fiscal opportunity and says it will make industries more efficient. He acknowledges risk only in passing, saying it should be managed responsibly, so he is mostly optimistic and not enthusiastic with risks dismissed.
just.agi_pilled: He talks about AI's economic benefits and 'the next frontier' of technology, but never mentions AGI, superintelligence, or the scale of AI's long-term transformation. There is nothing on this dimension to score.
just.x_risk: He says only that risk should be 'managed responsibly' and that 'zero risk means we lose'. He names no catastrophic or everyday harms, so there is not enough to score.
just.china_race: Winning the AI race is a primary lens for him. He calls it an 'imperative' and says America, not China, will lead. He also says that demanding zero risk means losing, though he still nods to managing risk.
just.regulation: He says 'erring on the side of innovation' is the right initial posture and that zero risk means losing. He accepts responsible risk management but shows no support for specific rules, so he reads as light-touch.

members.summary: Arrington talks about AI mainly as an engine of economic growth, government efficiency, and investment in West Texas, where data centers and energy are central. He frames AI as a race the U.S. must win against China and favors erring on the side of innovation, while briefly noting that risk should be managed responsibly. He does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, or specific regulatory proposals.

members.name: Pramila Jayapal

just.ai_overall: She portrays AI mainly as a threat: companies are 'out of control,' chatbots have contributed to deaths, and the industry poses economic and surveillance harms. She grants once that AI can be used for good, but harms dominate overwhelmingly.
just.agi_pilled: She does not say in her own voice that AGI or transformative AI is coming. She mentions superintelligence mainly to say the industry uses the framing to dodge responsibility, and her remarks on scale concern money and market power rather than expected capabilities.
just.x_risk: She says in her own voice that AI could destroy humanity, calls AI companies a serious threat to our future, and proposes shutting down dangerous models and banning systems that could go rogue or create catastrophic risks. She treats this as a top-tier priority, though s72 also criticizes how industry uses 'superintelligence' framing.
just.china_race: She explicitly calls for working with China on global AI regulation, which rejects race framing. Her only other AI-and-China-adjacent comment is about export controls.
just.regulation: She calls for comprehensive regulation: a mandatory federal AI charter that works like licensing, pre-approval testing, a kill switch, structural separation of AI from Big Tech, and shutdown of non-compliant firms. She also supports a data center moratorium and opposes state preemption.

members.summary: Jayapal frames AI mainly as a danger driven by concentrated Big Tech power, surveillance, discrimination, and unsafe chatbots, though she acknowledges potential benefits once. She has moved from civil-rights-focused guardrails to a sweeping National AI Charter that would license AI companies, ban risky systems, and break up Big Tech. She also warns that AI could destroy humanity, and she favors working with China on global rules rather than racing it.

members.name: Ron Estes

just.ai_overall: The only statement praises Wichita State's innovation in fields that include AI. It is boilerplate and does not say how he feels about AI itself.
just.agi_pilled: Nothing in the statement addresses how big or transformative AI will be, or AGI.
just.x_risk: The statement does not discuss any AI risks.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned.
just.regulation: The statement says nothing about AI regulation.

members.summary: The only statement is a 2020 congratulatory note on a NASA award to Wichita State. It mentions artificial intelligence in passing, alongside flight and space exploration. It reveals no view on AI policy, risks, or the future of the technology.

members.name: Ralph Norman

just.ai_overall: He says AI is 'a good thing and a bad thing' with potential to do a lot of damage, and he calls it too powerful. He also backs using it well (e.g., for veterans' healthcare), so his view is mixed and balanced.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a 'coming wave of technology' but never addresses AGI or how large or lasting its impact will be in a way that fits a level. The statements don't clearly speak to this dimension.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday harms such as imitated images and voices, harm to children, and data center costs. He also says AI could 'derail the country', but he gives no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He says Congress will have to put guardrails in place and that we should 'regulate what you can', mostly around harms to children and Americans. He also favors state and local control, and he wants data centers to pay their own way. This suggests targeted rules rather than a broad framework.

members.summary: Ralph Norman describes AI as both good and bad, powerful and potentially damaging. He supports Congress setting guardrails and regulating where possible, especially to protect children from deepfakes and voice imitation. He emphasizes state and local control over data centers and says the subject is complex and needs to be understood. He does not address AGI, catastrophic risk, or China in these statements.

members.name: Jimmy Gomez

just.ai_overall: He says technology can transform societies for the better, but his AI-specific statements are mostly about harms: facial recognition bias, algorithmic price discrimination, and threats to performers' likenesses. Harms dominate, with a nod to benefits.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AI's scale, future trajectory, or AGI. He only discusses specific uses and harms.
just.x_risk: His concerns are everyday harms: facial recognition bias and civil rights, price discrimination, and likeness rights. The 'threatening our lives' remark ties to law enforcement misidentification, not catastrophic or existential risk.
just.china_race: No statement mentions China or an AI race.
just.regulation: He backs specific protections such as performers' control of their likeness, scrutiny of facial recognition, and action against AI pricing abuse. He does not describe a broad framework.

members.summary: Gomez talks about AI mainly through specific harms: biased facial recognition, algorithmic price discrimination, and protecting actors' likenesses. He acknowledges that technology can benefit society if civil rights and liberties are protected. Many of his other AI mentions are political attacks on Trump's use of AI-generated images or on Musk, not statements of AI policy.

members.name: John R. Curtis

just.ai_overall: He says AI has enormous potential and the US should lead, while also warning of serious harms to kids, jobs, and possible catastrophe. Promise and risk are weighed about equally, with calls for guardrails.
just.agi_pilled: He expects AI to dramatically change employment and possibly eliminate whole job categories. He also refers to 'extraordinary analytical intelligence' and compares the risks to nuclear proliferation. He does not give AGI timelines or use the term AGI.
just.x_risk: He warns of catastrophic harm in bio, nuclear, and cyber domains. He says AI 'without human control' is dangerous and wants systems to 'remain fully under human control', and he likens the risks to nuclear proliferation. This goes beyond misuse to loss of control.
just.china_race: He says the US must continue to lead and keep its competitive edge. He is skeptical of a Chinese AI model and frames it as a CCP influence threat. China is a recurring but balanced theme alongside safety and accountability.
just.regulation: He backs targeted bipartisan bills on chatbots and kids, training-data transparency, and AI content labeling. He explicitly avoids creating a new federal regulator, so this is targeted rules rather than a broad framework.

members.summary: Curtis describes AI as having enormous potential and says the US must lead. He pairs that with warnings about child safety, job disruption, and catastrophic risks if systems are not under human control. He favors targeted bipartisan legislation and public hearings over a new regulator, and he treats China as a concern within that frame.

members.name: Tina Smith

just.ai_overall: She acknowledges AI's potential (a "game-changer," "great potential"), but most of her statements stress harms, corporate power, bubble risk and the need for accountability. Harms dominate her framing.
just.agi_pilled: She does not say how large or lasting AI's impact will be. She touches on frontier AI and a bubble, but never addresses AGI or the scale of transformation.
just.x_risk: She calls for a mutual US-China slowdown in AI development and is wary of frontier AI. She also raises biosecurity in a hearing question. That suggests serious large-scale risk concerns, but she never explicitly names loss of control or extinction.
just.china_race: She wanted a comprehensive agreement with China for a mutual slowdown of AI development, which is cooperation rather than race framing. She also mocks the Republican "compete with China" argument for data centers.
just.regulation: She wants AI companies held civilly and criminally liable, says they cannot self-regulate, and calls for Congress to create AI guardrails and for bipartisan AI safety measures. This is substantial regulation, though she does not specify licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Tina Smith talks about AI mainly as a matter of corporate accountability and power. She is critical of Big Tech and AI executives, wants companies held liable, and opposes self-regulation. She acknowledges AI's potential, especially in housing and health, but stresses bias, opacity, a possible financial bubble, and the risk of harm. She favors a US-China mutual slowdown over a race.

members.name: Cindy Hyde-Smith

just.ai_overall: She mostly frames AI as an economic and national-security opportunity for Mississippi, with brief mentions of privacy and cybersecurity risks that she treats as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AGI, transformative AI, or how large or lasting AI's impact will be. She talks only about specific investments and uses.
just.x_risk: She mentions only privacy and cybersecurity in passing and 'guardrails' for national security use. None of this is catastrophic framing, and none of it addresses catastrophic or existential risk.
just.china_race: China appears once, in a single clause saying America should lead AI 'not China'. It is not a recurring theme.
just.regulation: She supports targeted measures: guardrails for national security AI, privacy and cybersecurity protections, and rules making data centers pay for their own grid costs. She does not back broad AI frameworks.

members.summary: Hyde-Smith talks about AI mainly as an economic development opportunity for Mississippi, covering data centers, jobs, agriculture, manufacturing and defense. She notes a few concerns, such as privacy, cybersecurity and ratepayer costs from data centers, and says America should lead on AI rather than China. Her policy interest is in targeted guardrails and energy-cost protections, not broad regulation or long-term AI risk.

members.name: Michael Cloud

just.ai_overall: He sees AI as an opportunity for the economy, infrastructure and human capability, and says the US must lead. He also acknowledges serious risks and wants guardrails, but treats them as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AGI, superintelligence, or how large or lasting AI's transformation will be. The statements cover strategy, R&D and data centers only.
just.x_risk: He raises the 'dangerous potential' of AI in the hands of adversaries with nefarious objectives, which is a national-security-scale concern. He also mentions unintended consequences, but never loss of control or existential risk.
just.china_race: He says 'We are certainly in an AI race against China' and repeatedly stresses staying ahead of adversaries, with speed and energy as the keys. He still pairs this with guardrails and with doing data centers 'right', so it is not dominant over all other concerns.
just.regulation: He favors guardrails, ethical guidelines and trustworthy, safe AI, and wants data centers built responsibly with local control. These are general or targeted measures rather than a broad regulatory framework.

members.summary: Michael Cloud describes AI mainly as a strategic and economic opportunity that the US must lead, and he often frames it as a race against China and other adversaries. He supports R&D, workforce preparation, and ethical guardrails, and he warns about misuse by hostile powers. Recently he has focused on energy and data centers, saying they should be built responsibly, with their own power and water and with local input.

members.name: Troy Balderson

just.ai_overall: He celebrates AI projects by students and calls AI an 'AI revolution' to be powered and won. He names no real risks, which suggests he sees AI mainly as an opportunity.
just.agi_pilled: 'AI revolution' is a passing phrase tied to energy needs. He says nothing about AGI or how large AI's long-term impact will be.
