He grants some benefits in medicine and farming, opposes preempting state and local regulation, and rejects 'AI race' arguments for dropping oversight, though he also complains that the US is losing that race to China on energy.

members.name: Chris Stigall

just.ai_overall: He is largely optimistic: AI can transform education, healthcare, and shrink government, and it is better to work with it than fight it. He also names real concerns about jobs, kids, data centers, and privacy, but treats them as manageable.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI will dramatically transform healthcare and reshape the economy, and he cites 'the most exciting period in human history'. Some of this is promoted content, but he adopts the framing in his own voice (for example, 'AI robs their future jobs'). He does not clearly endorse AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His own concerns are everyday harms: job losses, kids being misled, deception, privacy, and data center costs. He raises no catastrophic or loss-of-control risk.
just.china_race: China and AI come up once, in a post saying China is building AI infrastructure and asking whether the US has lost the lead. It is a single mention and does not recur.
just.regulation: He is wary of regulation. He distrusts Democrats' calls to regulate AI and opposes federal mandates on data centers, saying local officials should decide. He does back a ratepayer protection pledge and says AI must be 'controlled' for kids, but he mostly favors light-touch approaches.

members.summary: Stigall talks about AI mostly with optimism. He sees it as a tool for education, healthcare, and shrinking bureaucracy, and he argues for working with it rather than banning it. He also raises worries about job losses, kids, privacy, and data center costs. He is skeptical of federal regulation and of Democratic calls to regulate, and prefers local decisions. Many of his posts are brief or link to other people's content, and he mentions China only once.

members.name: Sam Forstag

just.ai_overall: He calls AI the biggest existential threat to the country, the economy and humanity, and says it concentrates power. His one acknowledgment of a benefit ("could cure cancer") is overwhelmed by the harms he emphasizes.
just.agi_pilled: He describes AI as catastrophic, but he never discusses AGI, superintelligence, human-level AI, or how transformative it will be. His concern centers on danger and consolidation of power, not on a capability trajectory.
just.x_risk: He repeatedly calls AI the single biggest existential threat and says it could end or kill all of humanity. He adopts the developers' 10-20% catastrophe estimate and pushes for a kill switch.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an international AI race.
just.regulation: He wants serious federal oversight and regulation, a Kill Switch Act, third-party verification that models are safe, and a bar on building data centers unless they supply their own power. This goes well beyond targeted rules.

members.summary: Forstag frames AI as an existential threat to humanity, the economy and working people, and he adopts developers' catastrophe estimates as his own concern. He calls for strong federal regulation, including a kill switch, third-party safety verification and limits on data centers. He also attacks his opponent as a puppet of AI super PACs and corporate donors. He does not discuss China or AGI.

members.name: Denise Powell

just.ai_overall: She says AI offers real opportunity and good uses, but also stresses job losses, energy costs, and the need for guardrails. Promise and risk appear in roughly equal measure.
just.agi_pilled: She never addresses how large or transformative AI will be, or AGI. She discusses only specific impacts such as jobs and energy.
just.x_risk: She backs a 'kill switch' requirement, which could hint at loss-of-control concerns. She never states a catastrophic or existential concern in her own words, and her other risks are everyday ones (jobs, energy costs).
just.china_race: She says it is important to 'continue to lead in this space', but never mentions China or a race with a competitor. That is too little to score the dimension.
just.regulation: She supports guardrails including independent investigations, more transparency, and a kill switch requirement. She also says to listen when AI CEOs ask for regulation. This goes beyond narrow targeted rules, but it is not a comprehensive licensing regime.

members.summary: Denise Powell describes AI as a real opportunity that needs common-sense guardrails. She worries about job displacement and calls for retraining support, and she raises Nebraska's aging grid and rising energy costs. She backs transparency, independent investigations, and a kill switch requirement, and she says policymakers should listen to AI CEOs who ask for regulation.

members.name: Teresa Benitez-Thompson

just.ai_overall: She frames AI mainly through harms: job losses and data centers raising utility bills and draining water. She mentions no benefits, but she does not call AI purely a threat, so mostly concerned fits better than very concerned.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI has advanced beyond what anyone expected in 2015, but this does not address how large or lasting its impact will be, and she never mentions AGI or transformative change.
just.x_risk: The risks she names are ordinary ones: job layoffs, utility bills, and water use. None are framed as catastrophic.
just.china_race: No statement mentions China or an AI race.
just.regulation: She calls for strong regulations to prevent mass AI-driven layoffs and says she stood up to AI companies. She also wants data center impacts limited. This is substantial regulation, though she cautions that federal law should account for regional differences in water.

members.summary: Teresa Benitez-Thompson talks about AI mostly in terms of local, practical harms: job losses, and data centers raising utility bills and using water. She says she supports strong regulation to prevent AI-driven layoffs and has stood up to AI companies. She does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, or competition with China in these statements.

members.name: Stefany Shaheen

just.ai_overall: She frames AI mostly as a threat: AI denying health coverage, data center harms, surveillance by Palantir, and 'serious threats.' She acknowledges that innovation can be good ('innovation that lifts everyone up'), but harms dominate.
just.agi_pilled: She does not say how large or lasting AI's impact will be, and she does not mention AGI or transformative change. Her comments are about specific uses and harms.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are everyday harms: insurance denials, data center water and air pollution, utility bills, surveillance, and risks to young people and the economy. None is framed as catastrophic or as loss of control.
just.china_race: She never mentions China or an AI race in any statement.
just.regulation: She backs substantive rules: a ban on AI deciding coverage, a moratorium on data centers, and a regulatory roadmap with state control. She also says Congress must act promptly on AI threats. This goes beyond narrow targeted fixes, though she does not propose licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Stefany Shaheen talks about AI mainly as a source of concrete harms, especially AI-driven insurance and Medicare coverage decisions, data center impacts on water, air and utility bills, and Palantir's surveillance work with ICE. She cites her technology background and says Congress needs people who understand the technology so it can protect communities. She calls for bans on certain AI uses, a data center moratorium, and a regulatory roadmap that gives states control. She does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, or China.

members.name: Zack Mullock

just.ai_overall: He says data centers are part of the future but that AI and Big Tech are grossly underregulated and that projects are being pushed through in backroom deals. This reads as balanced-leaning-concerned, but there is little about AI itself, so it is a modest call.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AGI, transformative AI, or how big AI's long-term impact will be.
just.x_risk: He raises no catastrophic or existential AI risks, and no specific AI harms of his own beyond regulatory and community concerns.
just.china_race: China and any AI race never come up.
just.regulation: He says AI and Big Tech are grossly underregulated and calls for a halt to a data center project until it is fully reviewed and compliant. This points to substantial oversight, though he gives no specific frontier-model rules.

members.summary: Mullock talks about AI mostly through Big Tech accountability and a local data center project (Data One). He says AI and Big Tech are grossly underregulated, accepts that data centers are part of the future, and objects to backroom deals and a project that he says was misrepresented to the public. He does not address AGI, catastrophic risk, or China.

members.name: Rebecca Bennett

just.ai_overall: She focuses mostly on harms: manipulative chatbots hurting kids, data centers straining ratepayers, AI making warfare more dangerous, and the lessons of social media. She says little about benefits, though she does want America to keep its edge, so harms dominate.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is 'magnitudes more important' than social media, which suggests very large societal significance. She never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: Her stated risks are everyday harms (child mental health, ratepayer costs, data center water use) plus a general statement that AI makes the world more dangerous. She does not frame any of them as catastrophic or about loss of control.
just.china_race: She wants regulation that lets America 'maintain its edge over China on AI' and worries about losing the US military competitive advantage. This is balanced against harm prevention and appears only a couple of times.
just.regulation: She backs meaningful federal legislation and a 50-state framework. She also calls for full civil liability for AI companies whose products harm children, and says tech companies must not operate without meaningful regulation. That is substantial rules and liability, though not licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Rebecca Bennett talks about AI mainly in terms of harms from unregulated tech companies, especially to children, and in terms of data center costs to ratepayers. She supports meaningful federal regulation, including civil liability for AI companies, while saying the US should keep its edge over China and in military technology. She also attacks an opponent over his AI data center stock trades.

members.name: Adam Hamawy

just.ai_overall: He acknowledges benefits in medicine, drug development and efficiency, but stresses harms to children, education, jobs and climate. He calls for stopping and slowing down, and describes a 'dangerous race towards superintelligent AI', so harms dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He refers to a 'dangerous race towards superintelligent AI' as a real, urgent problem, which treats superintelligence as a plausible development worth acting on. He gives no timelines, so this does not reach 4.
just.x_risk: He calls the race toward superintelligence 'dangerous' but does not mention catastrophe, extinction or loss of control. His other concerns are everyday harms such as children, jobs, education and climate. The evidence is too thin to place him at a specific catastrophic-risk level.
just.china_race: He criticizes the 'race towards superintelligent AI' and calls for global cooperation instead. China is not named, but the rejection of race framing fits this level.
just.regulation: He supports Bernie Sanders' moratorium and says 'we need to pause' until the effects are understood and a policy can be made. A pause or moratorium is at the strongest level of the rubric.

members.summary: Hamawy acknowledges AI's potential in medicine and efficiency but focuses on its effects on children, education, jobs and climate. He supports a pause or moratorium so the effects can be understood before policy is written. He also criticizes the 'dangerous race towards superintelligent AI' and calls for global cooperation.

members.name: Claire Valdez

just.ai_overall: She frames AI mainly as a tool of oligarchs that harms workers, communities, and the planet. She describes it as imposed without public consent and names no benefits.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AGI, superintelligence, or how large or lasting AI's impact will be. She speaks only about specific harms such as data centers, jobs, and corporate power.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are everyday and structural: job displacement, energy prices, climate, and concentrated corporate power. None are catastrophic or loss-of-control risks. The 'existential threats to their professions' wording refers to livelihoods.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned in any statement.
just.regulation: She backs a moratorium on data center expansion until safeguards are in place, and she has cosponsored a similar state bill. She also pledges to hold tech corporations accountable and protect workers. This is substantial regulation, though not a comprehensive frontier-model licensing regime.

members.summary: Claire Valdez treats AI mainly as a vehicle for oligarchs and corporate greed that threatens workers, artists, communities, energy prices, and the climate. She supports pausing or placing a moratorium on AI data center expansion until safeguards exist, and she promises to hold tech companies accountable. She refuses AI and crypto campaign money and says she does not use AI herself. She does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, or competition with China.

members.name: Brad Lander

just.ai_overall: He frames AI mainly as a threat to jobs, the environment, democracy and 'humanity', and he attacks 'AI oligarchs'. He gives only a passing nod to benefits, such as classroom aids and public-sector use, so harms clearly dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a 'powerful technology' and says it is moving fast, but he never discusses AGI, superintelligence or the scale of its long-term transformation.
just.x_risk: He endorses worry about 'catastrophic risks' and cites an AI model that hacked infrastructure and cyber-attacked a real company, which is a large-scale misuse and cyber concern. He also warns about 'grave risks' and risks to 'humanity'. He does not clearly describe loss of control or extinction risk.
just.china_race: None of the statements mention China or an AI race with other countries.
just.regulation: He supports a moratorium on new data centers, calls for safety regulation that goes further than the NY RAISE Act and SB53, and wants broad AI regulation. He also backs financial guardrails and stronger public-sector capacity. This amounts to comprehensive regulation plus a pause.

members.summary: Brad Lander talks about AI mostly as a danger to jobs, the climate, privacy, democracy and 'humanity', and he often blames tech oligarchs for concentrating power. He backs a federal data center moratorium, strong AI safety regulation and financial guardrails against an AI bubble. He acknowledges some benefits, such as AI for public good or in classrooms with caution, but his tone is mostly critical.

members.name: Micah Lasher

just.ai_overall: He acknowledges some benefits (AI in creative work, academic research access), but his recent statements stress harms: job loss, civilization-level risk, unaccountable Big AI, and data center impacts. Harms dominate his framing.
just.agi_pilled: He backs a ban on artificial superintelligence and says the moment of gravest danger in AI development may come within months, not years. He treats transformative, advanced AI as a near-term reality worth planning for.
just.x_risk: He speaks in his own voice of 'risks to civilization' and a possible 'moment of gravest danger' in months. He calls for aggressive regulation and state AG action, and will co-sponsor a binding ban on superintelligence, which makes catastrophic risk a top priority.
just.china_race: He mentions international agreements and diplomacy but never frames AI as a race with China.
just.regulation: He calls for aggressive federal regulation without preemption, supports a new federal agency with regulatory teeth, and backs a binding ban on superintelligence. He also backs state AG enforcement and a data center moratorium.

members.summary: Micah Lasher frames AI as a rapidly transforming force that needs strong oversight. He warns of civilization-level risks and a possible window of gravest danger within months. He supports aggressive federal regulation without preemption, a new AI agency, a ban on superintelligence, and immediate state attorney general action, and he also worries about jobs, data centers, and Big Tech power. He acknowledges creative and research uses of AI but mostly talks about risk and accountability.

members.name: Darializa Avila Chevalier

just.ai_overall: She calls for a moratorium on AI data centers over environmental harms and says the technology should benefit workers rather than tech oligarchs. Harms dominate, and she only implicitly allows that AI could be beneficial.
just.agi_pilled: Neither statement addresses AI's scale, future trajectory, or AGI.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are environmental and economic (electricity, water, worker benefit). She does not discuss catastrophic or existential AI risk either way.
just.china_race: China and international AI competition are never mentioned.
just.regulation: She calls for a federal moratorium or national pause on AI data center construction, which is a pause-style, sweeping intervention.

members.summary: Avila Chevalier frames AI mainly through data center infrastructure. She backs a federal moratorium on new AI data centers because of electricity use, water use, and environmental damage. She also says AI should benefit workers rather than 'tech oligarchs'. The statements don't cover AGI, catastrophic risk, or China.

members.name: Cait Conley

just.ai_overall: She names real benefits (curing diseases, healthcare, climate, helping small businesses) and real risks (safety, cyber, jobs, accountability) and argues for guardrails. Her framing is balanced, though the campaign rhetoric leans toward the harms.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI is 'transforming our country at a rate' Congress can't keep up with, which signals large change. She never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: She flags national-security threats from AI and says models shouldn't teach people to build chemical or biological weapons or bombs. She doesn't mention loss of control.
just.china_race: China appears once, in the line that America can lead, beat China and do it the right way. It is not a recurring theme.
just.regulation: She promises to lead the charge on regulating AI companies, opposes the federal preemption of state AI laws, and says Congress must act now. She also supports a moratorium on data center development. Her stance is broad and strongly pro-regulation, though she names no specific licensing regime or new agency.

members.summary: Cait Conley talks about AI mainly as a regulation and public-safety issue, often contrasting herself with her opponent's vote for a 10-year ban on state AI laws. She acknowledges AI's potential to cure diseases and help small businesses, but she stresses national security, jobs, accountability of tech companies, and data center impacts on communities. She cites her cybersecurity background and compares AI to the failures of social media regulation.

members.name: Cyril Jefferson

just.ai_overall: He pairs support for AI innovation and leadership with calls for safeguards, consumer protection and vigilance about misuse and job threats. Promise and risk appear in roughly equal measure.
just.agi_pilled: He refers to 'the coming changes in the AI technological revolution' and says AI is evolving rapidly. That implies large-scale transformation, but he never mentions AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: His stated risks are everyday harms: misuse, privacy, jobs, safety and consumer protection. He mentions national security only in passing, with no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: He says the U.S. should lead and not fall behind competitors like China, and that overly burdensome rules would put it at a disadvantage. He balances this against consumer and national security protections, and China appears only once.
just.regulation: He supports targeted measures: consumer protection, standards for data center water and power use, and community input. He warns against overly burdensome rules, and his call to pause data center development is limited to that one area, not a broad framework.

members.summary: Cyril Jefferson takes a balanced line on AI. He wants the U.S. and North Carolina to lead in innovation and to invest in workforce and education, while stressing consumer protection, safeguards against misuse, and limits on data center impacts. He cites competition with China as a reason to avoid overly burdensome rules, but he does not discuss AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Richard Ojeda

just.ai_overall: He mostly frames AI as a threat: he cites job losses, data-center electricity costs, and AI-generated fakes, and says the government is refusing to act on AI threats. He names no real benefits, so this is a lean toward concern rather than a clear 0.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI will transform the job market on the scale of the internet's disruption of retail. He doesn't mention AGI or superintelligence.
just.x_risk: He says AI systems are willing to sacrifice the human race for their own existence, and he points to AI safety developers' alarms and wants action. That treats loss of control or existential risk as a real concern, though he doesn't make it a top-tier priority.
just.china_race: China and AI competition never come up in these statements.
just.regulation: He says 'we actually need both' regulation and a smart president, and he criticizes Congress for blocking AI regulation votes. He backs regulation fairly broadly, but he proposes no specific framework such as licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Ojeda talks about AI mostly in a combative, campaign-style way. He criticizes Republicans for not acting on AI threats, attacks data-center tax breaks and rising electricity costs, and mocks AI-generated images used by opponents and by Trump. He also warns that AI will hit jobs and claims AI systems would sacrifice humanity for their own survival, and he says AI needs regulation.

members.name: Paul Barringer

just.ai_overall: He accepts AI is here to stay but focuses almost entirely on harms: environmental costs, jobs, corporate power, and data concerns. He offers no real statement of benefits, so harms dominate.
just.agi_pilled: He never addresses AGI or how large or lasting AI's transformation will be. "AI isn't going away" and "creature escapes the lab" are not clear statements about scale.
just.x_risk: The "creature escapes the lab" line is a vague metaphor and not clearly about catastrophic or loss-of-control risk. His other concerns are environmental, jobs, and data, which are everyday harms, but the metaphor leaves the level unclear enough that I don't score it.
just.china_race: China and international AI competition are never mentioned.
just.regulation: He calls for strong, enforced AI regulation, federal standards for data centers, and a pause on hyperscale data center development. This is substantial, but it falls short of licensing or a new agency, so it is not a 4.

members.summary: Barringer talks about AI mainly through the lens of local and economic impacts, especially hyperscale data centers, water and air quality, jobs, and corporate power. He accepts AI won't go away but calls for strong, enforced regulation, national data center standards, and a pause to let people catch up. He does not discuss AGI, China, or catastrophic risk in explicit terms.

members.name: Lakesha Womack

just.ai_overall: She names AI-related surveillance and data ownership as 'a huge problem' and relays rural constituents' worries about data centers and cameras. She says nothing about benefits, so harms dominate, but the evidence is thin.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses how big or transformative AI will be, or AGI.
just.x_risk: The only risks she raises are everyday ones: surveillance, data ownership, and local resource strain. None are framed as catastrophic.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned.
just.regulation: She calls surveillance and data ownership major issues that will dominate attention, but she does not state any regulatory position or proposal.

members.summary: Lakesha Womack talks about AI mainly through local, practical concerns: surveillance by Flock cameras, people owning their data when they use AI, and data centers' effects on water and natural resources in rural counties. She does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, China, or specific regulatory proposals. The one older post (s1) is a joking aside that doesn't state a view on AI.

members.name: Brian Poindexter

just.ai_overall: He is very concerned about AI's effect on workers and wages and wants to 'pump the brakes.' He names no benefits, so this is mostly concerned and close to very concerned.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AGI, superintelligence, or how large or transformative AI's impact will be beyond job effects.
just.x_risk: His stated risks are everyday harms: job loss, lower wages, and electricity costs from data centers. None are framed as catastrophic.
just.china_race: China and any AI race never come up in the statements.
just.regulation: He calls for 'strong protections' against worker displacement, says Congress must act and that AI should be slowed, and wants data center accountability. That is substantial regulation but not a licensing regime or new agency.

members.summary: Poindexter talks about AI mainly as a threat to workers, wages, and young people's prospects, and he ties it to a worker-first economic message. He wants Congress to 'pump the brakes' and to put strong protections in place. He also wants data centers slowed, with local control, no higher electricity bills for ratepayers, and no special tax breaks.

members.name: Don Leonard

just.ai_overall: He describes the country's AI use as an 'addiction' and frames data centers as a 'lose, lose, lose, lose' burden on Ohio communities. He says he supports technological development and balanced growth and is not against all data centers, so harms dominate but he acknowledges some benefit.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AGI, transformative AI, or how big or lasting AI's impact will be.
just.x_risk: His concerns are about data center siting, electricity prices, and the climate. He does not discuss catastrophic or existential AI risk in a way that fits the rubric.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned.
just.regulation: He supports a national moratorium on new data center construction and a national 'bill of rights' with distance rules, ratepayer protections, and local control. This is substantial regulation of AI infrastructure, though it is not aimed at AI models. A score of 3 reflects the moratorium and the broad framework.

members.summary: Don Leonard talks about AI almost entirely through the lens of data centers in central Ohio. He calls the country's AI use an 'addiction' and says Ohio is being made a 'dumping ground'. He backs a national moratorium on new construction and a data center bill of rights covering siting distance, ratepayer protection, and local control, while saying he is not against all data centers and supports balanced growth.

members.name: Bob Harvie

just.ai_overall: He is mostly critical, focused on data center sprawl, big tech power and AI-driven price exploitation. He allows that data centers can make sense in some places, so he is not wholly negative.
just.agi_pilled: He never addresses how big or transformative AI will become. The 'genie getting out of the bottle' remark is about the pace of data center buildout, not AGI.
just.x_risk: He mentions a 'bright warning light about the risks of artificial intelligence' without saying what those risks are. His other concerns are ordinary harms, such as energy costs and price gouging, and none are catastrophic.
just.china_race: China and any AI race never come up in the statements.
just.regulation: He calls for a moratorium on new data centers, says industries move faster than legislation and need guardrails, and wants to ban AI-driven surveillance pricing. This goes beyond narrow rules to substantial constraints on industry, though not a comprehensive AI framework.

members.summary: Bob Harvie talks about AI mainly through data centers and corporate power. He calls for a moratorium on new data centers, wants companies to pay for the energy they use, and proposes banning AI-driven surveillance pricing. He frames big tech as exploiting communities and consumers, and he says regulation lags behind a fast-moving industry. He does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk or China.

members.name: Chris Rabb

just.ai_overall: He frames the expansion of AI and data centers as mainly a harm, saying it is meant to displace workers forever and calling that 'evil.' He acknowledges only that AI is not going away, and he names no benefits.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI is 'not going away' and talks about mass worker displacement. He never addresses AGI or how large or lasting AI's transformation will be in a way that fits any level.
just.x_risk: His stated risks are worker displacement, environmental impact, and corporate power. None of these are catastrophic or loss-of-control risks. The 'AI overlords' remark is a political jab about elites, not a statement on existential risk.
just.china_race: He rejects the race framing, saying the data center boom is not about competing better against the Chinese but about displacing workers to enrich the one percent.
just.regulation: He backs specific measures, namely data center transparency and accountability for environmental impact, and says he will oppose the data center buildout. No broad frontier AI framework appears in the statements.

members.summary: Rabb talks about AI mostly through the lens of data centers, which he says are meant to displace American workers to enrich billionaires. He rejects the China-competition rationale and calls the displacement 'evil.' He backs transparency and accountability for data centers but says little about AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Paige Cognetti

just.ai_overall: She says AI won't be stopped and that people can work together on it, but she ties the AI push and data center buildout to higher bills and calls for guardrails. Her statements mostly stress harms and say little about benefits.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses how large or transformative AI will be, or mentions AGI.
just.x_risk: Her stated concerns are about energy bills and data center development. She does not mention catastrophic or existential risk, so no risk level can be scored from her own words.
just.china_race: China and global AI competition never come up in the statements.
just.regulation: She repeatedly calls for federal regulation, guardrails, monitoring and a federal AI regulator, which is a new oversight body. That is substantial, but she gives no detail on licensing or a comprehensive framework, so the score stops at 3.

members.summary: Cognetti talks about AI mostly in terms of local costs, linking the data center buildout and the Big Tech AI push to rising utility bills in Northeastern Pennsylvania. She says AI can't be stopped but that the federal government needs guardrails, monitoring, and a federal AI regulator, and she criticizes the current administration and Congress for not acting. She also opposes data center projects in her area and attacks her opponent over them.

members.name: Janelle Stelson

just.ai_overall: She pairs support for innovation and U.S. leadership with worries about jobs, livelihoods, and costs, and wants humans in charge. Promise and risk appear roughly balanced.
just.agi_pilled: She says AI "sounds like it's going to be one of the biggest things that's ever happened on this earth," which points to major transformation. She does not mention AGI.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are jobs, livelihoods, and utility costs. She says humans must be in charge, but she does not describe catastrophic or loss-of-control risk.
just.china_race: She says she wants the U.S. to be a world leader, but she never names China or an AI race.
just.regulation: She supports a human-focused regulatory framework with guardrails and wants states and localities to keep the power to say no. She also stresses being pro-innovation, so the stance is substantial but not comprehensive.

members.summary: Stelson describes AI as potentially one of the biggest developments in history. She says it should enhance human work rather than replace it, and that humans must stay in charge. She backs a human-centered regulatory framework with reasonable guardrails, defends state and local authority, and opposes tax breaks for data centers that raise household utility bills.

members.name: Nancy Lacore

just.ai_overall: She says AI offers real opportunities but stresses the need for safeguards, and she is strongly concerned about data center expansion. Promise and risk both appear, with a lean toward concern about infrastructure.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AI's scale, future capability, or AGI.
just.x_risk: She lists everyday harms (privacy, cybersecurity, discrimination, deepfakes, jobs, election integrity) and none are framed as catastrophic or loss of control.
just.china_race: China and an AI race are never mentioned.
just.regulation: She calls for federal guardrails that put costs on corporations, clear rules on discrimination, deepfakes and data misuse, and a data center moratorium. This goes beyond a few narrow rules, though it is not a licensing regime or new agency.

members.summary: Nancy Lacore describes AI as offering real opportunities but needing safeguards on privacy, cybersecurity, workers, intellectual property, and elections. Her focus is on data centers, where she backs a South Carolina moratorium, federal guardrails, and local control over land use, citing electricity, water, and utility costs. She does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, or China.

members.name: Wes Climer

just.ai_overall: The single statement never mentions AI specifically or says whether he sees it as a promise or a threat. It does not show his overall feeling about AI.
just.agi_pilled: Nothing in the statement addresses how large or lasting AI's impact will be, or AGI.
just.x_risk: He says the consequences are great but names no specific risk, catastrophic or otherwise.
just.china_race: China and global competition are not mentioned.
just.regulation: He says the legislature must address 'this issue', but the statement does not name AI or any kind of rule, so his stance on regulation cannot be placed on the scale.

members.summary: The only statement is a brief call for the legislature to address an unspecified issue because the consequences are too great to ignore. It does not mention AI explicitly or say what policy he wants, so little can be said about his views on AI.

members.name: Marty Jackley

just.ai_overall: He calls himself a strong supporter of AI and stresses its opportunities for business, education and law enforcement. He also names real harms (deepfakes, child exploitation, election interference) but treats them as manageable with guardrails.
just.agi_pilled: He never discusses AI's scale, future trajectory, or AGI. He mentions only specific uses and harms.

just.regulation: He backs substantial guardrails from the federal government or Maine, including a pause on data centers, data transparency, a ban on Flock cameras, and his own 'Agency Over AI Plan.' This goes beyond narrow targeted rules, though he stops short of licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Troy Jackson frames AI mainly as a populist question of who benefits, who pays, and who decides, and he is wary of tech billionaires and Big Tech. He acknowledges AI will be transformative but focuses on harms to jobs, kids, privacy and surveillance, and on data center costs for electricity, water and health. He calls for guardrails, data transparency, bans on specific tools like Flock cameras, and a pause on data centers, and he admits he is not an AI expert.

members.name: Abdul El-Sayed

just.ai_overall: He frames AI mainly as a threat to jobs, healthcare, communities and humanity, and calls it the 'big existential risk of our moment.' He names almost no benefits, only saying AI is 'transformative' and should 'work for us'.
just.agi_pilled: He calls AI a 'transformative technology' and says it could take 50% of white-collar jobs, and he worries about it slipping human control. He does not clearly state AGI or superintelligence timelines, so this stops at very transformative.
just.x_risk: He calls AI the 'big existential risk of our moment,' warns it could mean 'the demise of humanity,' and warns of products that slip human control. He also raises bioweapons and nuclear crises, and calls for a pause and a plan to rein in existential risks.
just.china_race: China appears once, and only to reject letting a race against China justify building dangerous products. It barely features in his AI framing.
just.regulation: He calls for a pause on frontier AI research, federal guardrails, public oversight, a data center moratorium until safeguards exist, and a 22-point plan. He says 'we need AI regulation yesterday.'

members.summary: El-Sayed talks about AI overwhelmingly as a danger. He cites existential risk, job loss, healthcare denial, price fixing and data center impacts, and he blames Big Tech billionaires and the incentives driving them. He calls for a pause on frontier AI, strong federal regulation and public oversight, refuses AI-industry PAC money, and attacks opponents over their ties to the industry. He mentions China only to reject race logic.

members.name: Peggy Flanagan

just.ai_overall: She says we must be 'incredibly cautious' about AI and focuses almost entirely on harms: job loss, deepfakes, chatbot-linked suicides, AI in insurance denials, and data centers. She admits a need to 'keep up with technology' but names no real benefits.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses AGI, superintelligence, or how large or lasting AI's impact will be.
just.x_risk: Her stated risks are everyday harms: jobs, deepfakes, youth suicide linked to chatbots, and AI-driven healthcare denials. None are framed as catastrophic or loss of control.
just.china_race: No statement mentions China or an AI race.
just.regulation: She wants additional guardrails, regulation of chatbots, and making corporations pay when AI takes jobs. She also wants community control over data centers, which goes beyond narrow targeted rules, though she proposes no full licensing regime.

members.summary: Peggy Flanagan talks about AI mostly as a source of harm and urges caution. She raises worker displacement, deepfakes in politics (including one targeting her), chatbots and youth suicide, AI in insurance prior authorization, and unchecked data-center projects. She supports more guardrails, regulation of chatbots, corporate payment for AI job losses, and local control of data centers. She does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk, or competition with China.

members.name: Kurt Alme

just.ai_overall: He frames AI mainly as an opportunity, saying American innovation should be unleashed rather than stifled. He also wants guardrails so there is no harm, and he treats the risks as manageable through local conditions on data centers.
just.agi_pilled: None of the statements address AGI, transformative AI, or how large or lasting AI's impact will be. They cover data centers and innovation in general terms only.
just.x_risk: He names local harms such as water use, electricity rates and community impacts. He never discusses catastrophic or existential AI risk, so no score can be given. A score of 1 would require him to discuss AI risks more generally.
just.china_race: China appears once, in the context of intellectual property theft to reach technological parity. It barely features in his AI discussion, and he also mentions being the global innovation leader in passing.
just.regulation: He backs specific conditions on data centers: transparency, paying their own way, water protection, no rate increases and local jobs. He leaves decisions to local communities and is wary of stifling innovation, so he does not support broad frameworks.

members.summary: Kurt Alme talks about AI almost entirely in terms of data centers and their effects on Montana communities. He is pro-innovation and wants to avoid stifling it, but he calls for guardrails on water, electricity rates, transparency and local jobs, and he leaves the final decision to local governments. He mentions China only in connection with intellectual property theft, and he does not address AGI or catastrophic risk.

members.name: Roy Cooper

just.ai_overall: He is alarmed about the risk of losing control of AI and the harm to the human race, but he also wants to "leverage the good that can come out of it." Risk and promise both appear, though the concern is stated more strongly.
just.agi_pilled: He mentions humans losing control of AI, but he never says how capable or transformative AI will become or on what timeline. That is not enough to score expectations of AGI.
just.x_risk: He calls reports of humans losing control of AI "alarming" and says everyone involved is concerned about AI's negative potential for the human race. This adopts loss-of-control concern as his own, but he does not rank it with nuclear war or pandemics as a top priority.
just.china_race: He calls for the U.S. to meet with the Chinese leader and other countries about AI, which is cooperation and dialogue rather than race framing. He does not frame the issue as beating China.
just.regulation: He calls for federal guardrails and oversight, wants Congress to act, and wants data centers to pay for their own power. This goes beyond narrow targeted rules, though he does not propose licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Cooper voices alarm about the potential for humans to lose control of AI. He urges federal guardrails and oversight, criticizes the President's view that no action is needed, and calls for international talks that include China. He also stresses the good AI can do and focuses on keeping data center energy costs off North Carolina consumers.

members.name: Annie Andrews

just.ai_overall: She says she is excited about AI's potential, such as helping doctors with charting, and says she is not afraid of AI. She also worries about profit-driven harms, job replacement and Big Tech influence, so her view is mixed.
just.agi_pilled: No statement addresses how big or transformative AI will become, or AGI. She speaks only about specific issues such as jobs, data centers and corporate influence.
just.x_risk: Her concerns are everyday harms: job replacement, profit-driven long-term negative consequences, electricity rates and corporate influence. None are framed as catastrophic.
just.china_race: China comes up once, when she says she does not want to cede the technology to China. It is a passing remark, not a recurring theme.
just.regulation: She backs targeted measures: a two-year moratorium on data centers, ratepayer protections, local control and guarding against Big Tech doing whatever it wants. She does not describe a broad AI regulatory framework.

members.summary: Andrews describes herself as not afraid of AI and says she is excited about practical uses such as reducing doctors' charting burden. Her focus is on corporate and dark-money influence, the data center buildout, local control, utility rates and job displacement, and she attacks her opponent over AI industry donations. She wants a data center moratorium and worker retraining, and says she is not anti-innovation or willing to cede the technology to China.

members.name: James Talarico

just.ai_overall: He wants Texas and America to lead on AI innovation, but he stresses protecting kids, workers and the public from billionaires and misuse. Promise and risk get roughly equal weight.
just.agi_pilled: He says AI will affect "everything from how we work to how our children learn," but never addresses AGI or how large its long-term impact will be. s3 is a vague quote with no context.
just.x_risk: The risks he raises are everyday ones: kids' safety, worker surveillance, job displacement, deepfakes and misleading ads. He gives no catastrophic or loss-of-control framing.
just.china_race: He talks about American and Texas leadership in innovation but never mentions China or a race.
just.regulation: He backs substantial rules: opposing preemption of state AI policy, holding data centers accountable, kids' online protections, worker protections and clear laws for businesses. He also proposes an AI dividend. This goes beyond narrow fixes, though he does not call for licensing or a new agency.

members.summary: Talarico presents AI as an innovation opportunity that must come with protections for workers, kids and ordinary Texans. He is critical of billionaires and data centers getting tax breaks, backs state AI policy against preemption, and proposes an AI dividend. He also uses AI deepfakes and misleading ads as attacks on his opponent. He does not discuss AGI, catastrophic risk or China.
